lesson_scope: Standard, double-angle, substitution, and parts integration of trigonometric functions with exact area and volume applications.

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: standard linear composite cosine integration.

walkthrough.text:
Apply the linear integral rule for cosine:
$$\int \cos(3x)\,dx = \frac{1}{3}\sin(3x) + c$$

Integrate directly using standard reciprocal derivatives:
$$\int \sec^2(4x)\,dx = \frac{1}{4}\tan(4x) + c$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: definite integration of linear composite sine function.

walkthrough.text:
Find the antiderivative:
$$\int_0^{\pi/4} \sin(2x)\,dx = \left[ -\frac{1}{2}\cos(2x) \right]_0^{\pi/4}$$

Substitute limits:
$$= \left(-\frac{1}{2}\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\right) - \left(-\frac{1}{2}\cos(0)\right) = 0 - \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{1}{2}$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: integrating tan^2(x) using Pythagorean identity.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Integration of tan^2 x via identity.

hints: Integrate term by term: $\int (\sec^2 x - 1)\,dx = \tan x - x$.

walkthrough.text:
Use identity $\tan^2 x = \sec^2 x - 1$:
$$\int_0^{\pi/4} \tan^2 x\,dx = \int_0^{\pi/4} (\sec^2 x - 1)\,dx$$

Integrate:
$$= \left[ \tan x - x \right]_0^{\pi/4} = \left(\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) - \frac{\pi}{4}\right) - (0 - 0) = 1 - \frac{\pi}{4}$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: integrating cos^2(x) via double-angle identity.

hints: Evaluate at lower limit $0$: $0 + 0 = 0$. The exact value is $\frac{\pi}{4}$.

walkthrough.text:
Substitute double angle identity:
$$\int_0^{\pi/2} \cos^2 x\,dx = \int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{1}{2}(1 + \cos 2x)\,dx$$

Integrate and evaluate limits:
$$= \left[ \frac{1}{2}x + \frac{1}{4}\sin 2x \right]_0^{\pi/2} = \left(\frac{\pi}{4} + \frac{1}{4}\sin\pi\right) - (0 + 0) = \frac{\pi}{4}$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Drill: reverse chain rule / substitution with cosine power.

hints: Notice that $\sin x$ is the derivative of $-\cos x$.
The integral becomes $-\int u^3\,du = -\frac{1}{4}u^4 + c = -\frac{1}{4}\cos^4 x + c$.

walkthrough.text:
Use substitution $u = \cos x \implies du = -\sin x\,dx$:
$$\int \sin x\cos^3 x\,dx = -\int u^3\,du = -\frac{1}{4}u^4 + c = -\frac{1}{4}\cos^4 x + c$$

ai_rubric.observable: Recognises reverse chain rule or substitution $u = \cos x, du = -\sin x\,dx$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Structured Core: double angle transformation of sin^2(2x) and exact area computation.

walkthrough.text:
Use double-angle identity for sine squared:
$$\sin^2(2x) = \frac{1 - \cos(4x)}{2} = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2}\cos(4x)$$

Integrate term by term:
$$\int \left(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2}\cos(4x)\right)dx = \frac{1}{2}x - \frac{1}{8}\sin(4x) + c$$

hints: Substitute upper limit: $\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) - \frac{1}{8}\sin(2\pi) = \frac{\pi}{4} - 0 = \frac{\pi}{4}$. Subtract lower limit $(0 - 0)$.

walkthrough.text:
Apply the fundamental theorem of calculus:
$$\text{Area} = \left[ \frac{1}{2}x - \frac{1}{8}\sin(4x) \right]_0^{\pi/2}$$

Evaluate limits:
$$= \left(\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) - \frac{1}{8}\sin(2\pi)\right) - (0 - 0) = \frac{\pi}{4} - 0 = \frac{\pi}{4}$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Structured Core: integration by parts with algebraic and trigonometric factor and exact evaluation.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Integration by parts on x cos(2x).

hints: Choose $u = x$ to differentiate and $v' = \cos(2x)$ to integrate.
Use $\int u v'\,dx = uv - \int v u'\,dx = \frac{1}{2}x\sin(2x) - \int \frac{1}{2}\sin(2x)\,dx$.

walkthrough.text:
Identify parts:
$$u = x \implies u' = 1$$
$$v' = \cos(2x) \implies v = \frac{1}{2}\sin(2x)$$

Apply the integration by parts formula:
$$\int x\cos(2x)\,dx = \frac{1}{2}x\sin(2x) - \int \frac{1}{2}\sin(2x)\,dx$$
$$= \frac{1}{2}x\sin(2x) - \left(-\frac{1}{4}\cos(2x)\right) + c = \frac{1}{2}x\sin(2x) + \frac{1}{4}\cos(2x) + c$$

ai_rubric.observable: Obtains $\frac{1}{2}x\sin(2x) + \frac{1}{4}\cos(2x) + c$ with all steps shown.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Definite evaluation of trigonometric parts integral.

walkthrough.text:
Substitute limits into the antiderivative:
$$\int_0^{\pi/4} x\cos(2x)\,dx = \left[ \frac{1}{2}x\sin(2x) + \frac{1}{4}\cos(2x) \right]_0^{\pi/4}$$

Calculate value at upper limit $\frac{\pi}{4}$:
$$\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) + \frac{1}{4}\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = \frac{\pi}{8}(1) + 0 = \frac{\pi}{8}$$

Calculate value at lower limit $0$ and subtract:
$$\left(0 + \frac{1}{4}\cos(0)\right) = \frac{1}{4}$$
$$\text{Value} = \frac{\pi}{8} - \frac{1}{4} = \frac{\pi - 2}{8}$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Structured Core: substitution integration of rational trigonometric expression and exact log area evaluation.

hints: Substitute into the integral: $\int \frac{\sin x}{2 + \cos x}\,dx = \int -\frac{1}{u}\,du$.

walkthrough.text:
Differentiate substitution variable:
$$u = 2 + \cos x \implies du = -\sin x\,dx \implies \sin x\,dx = -du$$

Substitute and integrate:
$$\int \frac{\sin x}{2 + \cos x}\,dx = -\int \frac{1}{u}\,du = -\ln|u| + c = -\ln(2 + \cos x) + c$$

ai_rubric.observable: Substitutes back to reach $-\ln(2 + \cos x) + c$.

hints: Set up the area integral: $\text{Area} = \int_0^\pi \frac{\sin x}{2 + \cos x}\,dx$.

walkthrough.text:
Apply the limits $0$ and $\pi$ to the antiderivative:
$$\text{Area} = \left[ -\ln(2 + \cos x) \right]_0^\pi$$

Substitute $x = \pi$ and $x = 0$:
$$= (-\ln(2 + \cos\pi)) - (-\ln(2 + \cos 0)) = -\ln(1) + \ln(3) = 0 + \ln 3 = \ln 3$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Structured Core: integration by parts on x sec^2(x) and exact area evaluation involving radicals and logs.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Integration by parts with sec^2 x.

hints: Set $u = x$ and $v' = \sec^2 x$. Then $u' = 1$ and $v = \tan x$.
Apply integration by parts: $\int x\sec^2 x\,dx = x\tan x - \int \tan x\,dx$.

walkthrough.text:
Identify parts:
$$u = x \implies u' = 1$$
$$v' = \sec^2 x \implies v = \tan x$$

Apply the integration by parts formula:
$$\int x\sec^2 x\,dx = x\tan x - \int \tan x\,dx = x\tan x - \ln(\sec x) + c$$

ai_rubric.observable: Sets $u = x, v' = \sec^2 x \implies u' = 1, v = \tan x$.
Applies formula to write $x\tan x - \int \tan x\,dx$.
Integrates $\tan x$ to $\ln(\sec x)$ to obtain $x\tan x - \ln(\sec x) + c$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Exact area under x sec^2 x curve.

hints: Set up the area integral: $\text{Area} = \int_0^{\pi/4} x\sec^2 x\,dx$.
Substitute lower limit: $0 - \ln(1) = 0$. Subtract to get $\frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{1}{2}\ln 2$.

walkthrough.text:
Substitute limits into the antiderivative:
$$\text{Area} = \left[ x\tan x - \ln(\sec x) \right]_0^{\pi/4}$$

Calculate at $x = \frac{\pi}{4}$:
$$\frac{\pi}{4}\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) - \ln\left(\sec\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right) = \frac{\pi}{4}(1) - \ln(\sqrt{2}) = \frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{1}{2}\ln 2$$

Subtract value at $x = 0$:
$$(0 - \ln(1)) = 0$$
$$\text{Area} = \frac{\pi}{4} - \frac{1}{2}\ln 2$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Structured Capstone: higher-power tangent reduction via Pythagorean identity and exact evaluation.

hints: Write $\tan^3 x = \tan x(\sec^2 x - 1) = \tan x\sec^2 x - \tan x$.
For $\int \tan x\sec^2 x\,dx$, use substitution $u = \tan x, du = \sec^2 x\,dx$ to get $\frac{1}{2}\tan^2 x$.

walkthrough.text:
Expand using Pythagorean identity:
$$\tan^3 x = \tan x(\sec^2 x - 1) = \tan x\sec^2 x - \tan x$$

Integrate each term:
$$\int \tan x\sec^2 x\,dx = \frac{1}{2}\tan^2 x$$
$$\int -\tan x\,dx = -\ln(\sec x)$$
$$\int \tan^3 x\,dx = \frac{1}{2}\tan^2 x - \ln(\sec x) + c$$

ai_rubric.observable: Combines results to obtain $\frac{1}{2}\tan^2 x - \ln(\sec x) + c$.

walkthrough.text:
Substitute limits into antiderivative:
$$I = \left[ \frac{1}{2}\tan^2 x - \ln(\sec x) \right]_0^{\pi/3}$$

Evaluate at $x = \frac{\pi}{3}$:
$$\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{3})^2 - \ln(2) = \frac{3}{2} - \ln 2$$

Subtract value at $x = 0$:
$$(0 - \ln 1) = 0 \implies I = \frac{3}{2} - \ln 2$$

questions.difficulty_reason: Structured Capstone: repeated integration by parts with quadratic-trigonometric product and exact area evaluation.

hints: 1st parts: $u = x^2, v' = \sin x \implies u' = 2x, v = -\cos x$.
2nd parts: $u = 2x, v' = \cos x \implies u' = 2, v = \sin x$.
Evaluate $\int 2x\cos x\,dx = 2x\sin x - \int 2\sin x\,dx = 2x\sin x + 2\cos x$.

walkthrough.text:
Apply 1st integration by parts:
$$u = x^2 \implies u' = 2x, \quad v' = \sin x \implies v = -\cos x$$
$$\int x^2\sin x\,dx = -x^2\cos x - \int (-2x\cos x)\,dx = -x^2\cos x + \int 2x\cos x\,dx$$

Apply 2nd integration by parts to $\int 2x\cos x\,dx$:
$$u = 2x \implies u' = 2, \quad v' = \cos x \implies v = \sin x$$
$$\int 2x\cos x\,dx = 2x\sin x - \int 2\sin x\,dx = 2x\sin x + 2\cos x$$

Combine all parts:
$$-x^2\cos x + 2x\sin x + 2\cos x + c$$

ai_rubric.observable: Applies 1st integration by parts: $-x^2\cos x + \int 2x\cos x\,dx$.
Applies 2nd integration by parts to $\int 2x\cos x\,dx = 2x\sin x - \int 2\sin x\,dx$.
Combines all terms to obtain $-x^2\cos x + 2x\sin x + 2\cos x + c$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Exact area calculation from double parts.

hints: Set up definite integral: $\text{Area} = \int_0^\pi x^2\sin x\,dx$.
Apply limits to $[-x^2\cos x + 2x\sin x + 2\cos x]_0^\pi$.

walkthrough.text:
Substitute limits into the result from part (a):
$$\text{Area} = \left[ -x^2\cos x + 2x\sin x + 2\cos x \right]_0^\pi$$

Evaluate at upper limit $x = \pi$:
$$-\pi^2\cos\pi + 2\pi\sin\pi + 2\cos\pi = -\pi^2(-1) + 0 + 2(-1) = \pi^2 - 2$$

Evaluate at lower limit $x = 0$ and subtract:
$$-(0) + 0 + 2\cos(0) = 2$$
$$\text{Area} = (\pi^2 - 2) - 2 = \pi^2 - 4$$

ai_rubric.observable: Applies limits to $[-x^2\cos x + 2x\sin x + 2\cos x]_0^\pi$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Structured Capstone: radical substitution integration applied to volume of revolution in exact surd form.

walkthrough.text:
Apply substitution $u = 1 + \sin x \implies du = \cos x\,dx$:
$$\int \cos x\sqrt{1 + \sin x}\,dx = \int u^{1/2}\,du$$

Integrate with respect to $u$:
$$= \frac{2}{3}u^{3/2} + c = \frac{2}{3}(1 + \sin x)^{3/2} + c$$

ai_rubric.observable: Substitutes back to reach $\frac{2}{3}(1 + \sin x)^{3/2} + c$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Volume of revolution using radical trigonometric integral.

hints: Recall that Volume $= \pi \int y^2\,dx = \pi \int_0^{\pi/2} \cos x\sqrt{1 + \sin x}\,dx$.
Use the result from part (a): $\pi \left[ \frac{2}{3}(1 + \sin x)^{3/2} \right]_0^{\pi/2}$.

walkthrough.text:
Set up volume of revolution formula:
$$V = \pi \int_0^{\pi/2} y^2\,dx = \pi \int_0^{\pi/2} \cos x\sqrt{1 + \sin x}\,dx$$

Substitute limits into antiderivative:
$$V = \pi \left[ \frac{2}{3}(1 + \sin x)^{3/2} \right]_0^{\pi/2}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Sets up volume integral $V = \pi \int_0^{\pi/2} y^2\,dx = \pi \int_0^{\pi/2} \cos x\sqrt{1 + \sin x}\,dx$.
